declarations.description:
CodeMirror, not a `<textarea>`. The textarea it replaces was the right call
while a sandbox only had to hold text: undo, selection, spellcheck
suppression, mobile keyboards, and screen-reader support all came from the
platform. What it could not do is highlight what it holds, number its lines,
or say where the cursor is, and a status bar reading line and column has to
ask something.

**On its own path.** This is `@helix-io/sandbox/editor` rather than part of
the barrel, because CodeMirror is around 110 KB over the wire where the rest
of this package is a few. A sandbox with no editable pane should not pay for
one, and neither should a site that registers its elements once.

The view is built once and reconfigured, not rebuilt. Replacing it on every
change would throw away the undo history, the scroll position, and the
selection, which is most of what an editor is.

`root` is the shadow root rather than the document, or CodeMirror puts its
stylesheet where this element cannot see it and the editor renders unstyled.

members.name: focus
members.description:
Moves focus into the text, not onto the host.

The host is not focusable: what a reader types into is CodeMirror's
contenteditable, several nodes down inside this shadow root. Without this,
`editor.focus()` from outside silently does nothing.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.name: highlightStyle
declarations.description:
How source is colored, in Helix tokens.

CodeMirror ships `defaultHighlightStyle`, which is a fixed set of hex values
and therefore one palette in both color modes: readable on white, wrong on
anything else. These are `--helix-color-syntax-*`, which resolve through
`light-dark()` like every other color in the system, so the editor follows
the page rather than declaring its own mode.

The palette is GitHub's, which is what the sandbox this replaces used, and
what most engineers already read without having to learn it.

A tag not named here inherits the editor's foreground. That is deliberate:
punctuation, operators and separators are structure a reader skims past, and
coloring them competes with the names that carry the meaning.

declarations.name: highlight
declarations.description:
Highlights a snippet, returning HTML with one span per token.

**A parser, not an editor.** CodeMirror's grammars are Lezer parsers and
parsing is a pure function of the text: `highlightCode` walks a tree and
hands back tokens. Nothing is mounted, no document is created, and this runs
on a server with no DOM at all, which is what lets a static page ship
highlighted code with no client JavaScript spent on it.

**Here rather than in `helix/styled`, and that is the whole point.** A code block
is a component and must not carry a parser: CodeMirror is about 4 MB
installed, and a `dependencies` entry is paid by every consumer whether or
not they import it. This package already carries those grammars for the
editor, so highlighting costs nothing new. `CodeBlock` renders a `<slot>`,
so the output of this drops straight into one and the component stays
dependency-free while its content is highlighted by the same grammars the
editor uses. A snippet on a reference page and the same snippet open in the
sandbox are then coloured by one source rather than two that agree by
coincidence.

`classHighlighter` emits Lezer's own `tok-` class names. Mapping those to
colours is the consumer's, because the classes are stable and the palette is
not: the site paints them from `--helix-color-syntax-*`.

declarations.name: shellLanguage
declarations.description: The shell grammar, with `command` mapped into the palette.

declarations.name: htmlToJsx
declarations.description: The example's markup, as the body of a React component.

declarations.name: jsxToHtml
declarations.description: The markup a JSX example stands for.

The specs are not rewritten for this. The same `*.dom.spec.ts` files that run
in CI are bundled for the browser with `bun:test` and the DOM helpers pointed
at a browser harness, so a spec deleted in the morning stops being reported
in the afternoon and there is no second suite to keep in step.

**A browser is the stricter environment, not the looser one.** The node
harness runs against happy-dom, which does not implement `attachInternals` at
all and has to be handed an inert stub, reports `:popover-open` as unmatched
for a popover that is open, and returns nothing from `assignedNodes({ flatten:
true })` where a browser returns the fallback. Each of those has already
produced a spec that passed while asserting the opposite of what ships. Here
they are the platform's own.

They run in a frame of their own rather than the preview's, because `mount`
replaces the document body for every test and would take the example with it.

**That frame is parked at the document root, not in this shadow root.** It is
a worker rather than anything to look at, and where it sits in the tree
decides whether it is laid out at all: inside the panel it was a descendant of
an inactive tab, so on any tab but this one it had `display: none` above it
and every rectangle inside it was zero. Specs that read geometry then passed
against nothing, which is the failure that looks most like success. Found by
putting a known misplacement back and watching the specs stay green.
